Is this a subtle move away from innocent until proven guilty to sensationalize stories? Is a police allegation any less an unproven allegation in a court of law?

Saying "police said" is hearsay when the actual allegation is being made by someone else. Police are very rarely witnesses to crimes. Police interview witnesses and collect evidence. When police talk to the press about an accused they are careful to say "allegedly". When someone then posts on Voat saying "police said" about a given person accused of a crime, they are being dishonest.
Instead of using the word "allegedly" in stories about possible criminals, some posters are now using the term "police said".
"police said" is more precise. "allegedly" could mean "I got my five year old cousin to say it"

Minority suspect = Police said

White = Allegedly (they don't even use that word sometimes)

It's pretty much the same thing, the meaning of "allegedly" that it's the claim of something which has not been proven. Cops lay the charges, so it is ultimately the police who make the allegation, then the proof comes in trial.

I attribute it more to the dumbing-down of the average reader, thinning of their lexicon of words. Soon most news will be written with emoticons.

If the reporter gets their information from the police, then how is printing "Police said" not the most accurate possible description?

I think "allegedly" and "accused" make the schmuck sound more guilty, especially with the way the police have been systematically discredited over the past 15-20 years.

Compare:

"M. Oliver is accused of child pornography, solicitation, child endangerment, and obscenity - charges which could carry up to 250 years in federal prison"

vs.

"Police said they found two Traci Lords videos on Mr. Oliver's laptop from when that lying skank was making movies at 17."

Can you link an example? Just on the surface I kind of like it; it specifies not only the allegation but the source of the allegation. What society needs to do is recognize that "[x] said" isn't confirmation of fact, but we already have trouble with that when it comes to the word "allegedly".

As a quick example, "Valve allegedly kills babies" gives less information than "Kotaku says Valve kills babies". It also puts consideration of the source back into the forefront of my mind when I read it.
